entry.title: Greg Kurtzer's Ginux is now a userspace kernel
entry.content:
Ginux is a configurable userspace kernel for isolated Linux compatibility instances. It runs as an ordinary Linux process and places an explicit, versioned contract between managed workloads and the host kernel.

Important

Ginux began as an independent Rust kernel that booted directly through UEFI and ran a Rocky Linux 10 userspace. That research phase is complete. Its final source is permanently preserved on the bootable-kernel branch and at the bootable-kernel-final tag. Active development now continues here as a userspace kernel.

The standalone-kernel experiment proved that an AI coding agent, directed by an experienced human through architecture, gates, and executable tests, could construct a new kernel capable of running meaningful Linux userspace. It also made the limits of that result obvious.

Linux is much more than source code. It is a stable interface, a development process, a global community, vendor and hardware alignment, and decades of compatibility and operational experience. Reimplementing kernel mechanisms does not reproduce that ecosystem, and competing with Linux was never the goal.

The more useful result is the boundary the experiment exposed. Linux must preserve a broad userspace ABI; as Linus Torvalds put it, “And we simply do not break user space.” The kernel regression documentation records that rule. Ginux can sit above Linux and deliberately offer a smaller contract to each managed instance. Before a managed syscall has a host effect, Ginux decides whether to emulate it, perform a validated mediated operation, or deny it.

Put bluntly: Linux must not break userspace; Ginux is designed to break the full Linux ABI guarantee deliberately and selectively. A instance receives only the capabilities and interface behavior its approved workload requires. Every departure is intended to be explicit, versioned, reviewable, and tested, rather than accidental incompatibility.

This pivot is also a result of the development method. AI made it practical to build disposable but executable prototype code, test an architectural idea, learn from the running system, and carry the valuable parts into a better design. The prototype was evidence, not an obligation to turn every experiment into a product.

Host Linux kernel `- host systemd (real PID 1) `- ginux (ordinary trusted host process) `- instance contract |- virtual processes and identities |- virtual descriptors and kernel views |- assigned devices and resources `- managed Rocky Linux userspace `- instance systemd (virtual PID 1)

Ginux supervises native x86-64 programs and intercepts managed syscalls before their host effect. Its central dispatcher resolves the instance contract and chooses one of three outcomes:

Emulate: answer entirely from Ginux-owned state. Mediate: validate and translate the request, then perform a narrow Ginux-owned host operation. Deny: return a configured Linux-compatible error or terminate the task.

The current implementation includes:

a security-focused x86-64 interpreter and a balanced native ptrace backend; strict, versioned instance configuration and lifecycle; a digest-pinned OCI root, immutable filesystem index, and bounded overlay; Ginux-owned process, credential, signal, synchronization, timer, and event models; virtual devices with explicit assignment, ownership, and revocation; and bounded virtual /proc, /sys, cgroup v2, mount, namespace, machine, and boot-identity views; a host-shared network backend that remains syscall-mediated; and a pinned Rocky Linux 10 systemd baseline that reaches multi-user.target, authenticates a managed console login, updates through Rocky's enabled repositories, and shuts the instance down cleanly.

This is a named compatibility baseline, not a claim of complete Linux or systemd compatibility. Its exact image, readiness marker, tests, evidence, and limitations are recorded in hdae/gates-todo/9-systemd-baseline.md.

Ginux is also being tested as a containment boundary for AI agents and other automated software that can execute commands, modify files, open network connections, and start additional processes. Instead of giving an agent the host's complete Linux ABI, an operator can place its process tree inside a instance whose kernel contract exposes only the operations and virtual resources required for the task.

The research goal is a reviewable boundary spanning syscalls, ioctls, filesystems, devices, networking, process authority, and virtual /proc and /sys state. For example, a contract may allow an agent to read time, inspect its own processes, and modify one assigned workspace while denying clock changes, host filesystem access, unapproved network listeners, and unrelated devices. Ginux can then audit the contract decisions made while the agent and its child processes run.

This is an active verification target, not a claim that Ginux is currently a production-grade agent sandbox. The contract inventory, configurable policy, adversarial tests, performance costs, and escape boundaries are tracked through the HDAE gates and must be demonstrated before stronger containment claims are made.

The userspace-kernel idea is established research and engineering territory. Ginux explores a particular point in that design space:

Approach Primary boundary Difference in emphasis Linux seccomp Filters host syscalls Restricts the existing ABI rather than defining a complete virtual contract User-Mode Linux Runs Linux as a host process Reuses a complete Linux kernel over virtual hardware gVisor Implements an application kernel in userspace Closely related model with different compatibility and performance goals Gramine Packages applications with a library OS Uses manifests and a library-OS boundary Proxos Routes calls between private and commodity OSes Makes trust placement configurable across the syscall interface Ginux Gives each instance a versioned kernel contract Treats the declared contract, virtual state, devices, resources, and lifecycle as one reviewable boundary

Ginux does not promise the complete Linux ABI. Compatibility claims apply only to named contracts, workloads, and executable evidence.

The reference development environment is macOS arm64. QEMU TCG boots a pinned Rocky Linux 10 x86-64 host where Ginux runs as an ordinary unprivileged process. The host systemd remains real PID 1.

Check prerequisites:

make doctor

Prepare the pinned assets with explicit network operations:

make host-image-fetch make image-helper-fetch make instance-image-fetch make systemd-image-fetch

Build and run the deterministic suite offline after the caches are populated:

make build make check make test

Inspect the latest completed capability directly:

make test-systemd # cached image, external networking disabled make bench-prepare # one-time networked setup for the pinned benchmark image make bench # matched native/Ginux matrix plus mandatory budget checks make bench-modes-prepare # one-time setup for the three-way dispatch comparison make bench-modes # native/selective/paranoid tables and graphs make demo-gate-15 # bounded reproducible three-way comparison make test-systemd-live # shared network plus real upstream dnf -y update make host-run # general interactive Rocky host with Ginux installed make host-reset # discard that host's cache, instances, and writable state make demo-gate-9 # Gate 9 checkpoint through the same host workflow

Instance recipes select syscall control under [contract.syscalls]:

[contract.syscalls] control = "selective" # default; use "paranoid" for all-syscall mediation default = "deny" allow = ["*"] deny = []

selective is the default and permits direct host execution only when the instance contract allows the operation and Ginux's versioned catalog independently classifies it as direct-safe. Denials, virtual state, inspection, translation, emulation, pointer or descriptor validation, and modified results remain Ginux-dispatched in both modes. paranoid is an explicit opt-in that sends every syscall through the Ginux userspace dispatcher before completion.

make bench-compare checks every row against the 4% native budget and, after an accepted baseline is published under benchmarks/gate11/, against that Ginux baseline as well. Environment mismatches are reported separately from performance regressions. make demo-gate-11 runs a bounded human-inspectable comparison and returns nonzero when a mandatory row misses its budget.

Gate 15 provides a separate characterization workflow across native Rocky, selective Ginux, and paranoid Ginux. Native is the no-mediation control, not a Ginux instance mode. The checked-in templates under benchmarks/gate15/ fix the complete test protocol and may be copied without editing scripts. make bench-modes produces paired raw samples, metadata, a Markdown table, and an SVG graph under build/gate15/. See Reproducible performance measurement for the exact protocol, customization workflow, output schema, and interpretation limits.

make host-run boots the QEMU Rocky host and logs you into its ordinary shell. Ginux is installed in PATH. The first create or import downloads and verifies the pinned Rocky OCI image with live per-layer progress; later operations reuse the cache. The writable Rocky host overlay persists across make host-run, ordinary cleanup, builds, and tests, so cached images, instance definitions, roots, and stopped status remain available. make host-reset is the explicit destructive operation that stops the host and removes that overlay; the next make host-run starts from the pinned clean Rocky image. A complete first session is:

ginux create rocky ginux list ginux status rocky ginux start rocky --attach

create starts from the documented default recipe. Use ginux import NAME FILE to create or atomically replace an instance from a self-contained recipe, ginux export NAME to print that recipe, and ginux edit NAME to validate and atomically apply an editor session.

Instances are contract-locked by default. For an explicit maintenance window, stop the instance, run ginux unlock NAME, perform the required maintenance, stop it again, and run ginux lock NAME. ginux list and ginux status NAME show the current state, and starting an unlocked instance prints a warning. Unlocking relaxes configurable recipe restrictions only; Ginux still owns the virtual kernel boundary, rejects unsupported authority, reduces host identity, and applies NoNewPrivs. Lock state is host deployment state and is never written into an exported portable recipe.

Syscall auditing is disabled by default with [audit] enabled = false. Add --audit to ginux start to enable it for that run, or set enabled = true to enable it for every start. Enabled audit records always go to the instance's audit.log; they are kept separate from the attached console. Existing recipes using mode = "stderr" or mode = "disabled" remain read-compatible and normalize to the new boolean form when rewritten.

The instance specification supports typed recipe overrides, ingress and egress contract policy, volumes, virtual identity, and ordered pre-boot hooks. Host network attachment and translated ports are deployment settings, supplied as repeatable flags when the instance is created or changed:

ginux import web /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml \ --network eth0:1 \ --forward protocol=tcp,external_port=8080,instance_port=80 \ --forward protocol=tcp,external_port=8443,instance_port=443 ginux set web \ --network default \ --forward none

Omitting --network uses the host's default network. Multiple flags are validated and persisted atomically; an invalid combination changes nothing. Hooks run only as mediated instance processes; Ginux does not support arbitrary host-context hooks. See Gate 9.75 instance specification for the schema, precedence rules, examples, and verification targets.

The same instance file contains a self-contained hierarchical contract under [contract] and its syscalls, filesystem, network, devices, privileges, process, and kernel subsections. Syscall names accept bounded globs compiled against the pinned catalog; explicit denies always win. The contract is part of the instance rather than a separate operator object. Validate and inspect the complete instance recipe before launch:

ginux validate /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml ginux inspect /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml ginux explain /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml filesystem.path.write

See Self-contained userspace contract for the syntax, precedence, migration behavior, and complete CLI workflow.

The attached terminal becomes the Ginux instance console. Log in as root with password ginux, explore normally, press Ctrl-] to detach while leaving the instance running, and run kill -RTMIN+4 1 as instance root to shut down systemd and return to the host. Detached operation uses ginux start rocky, ginux status rocky, and ginux stop rocky. Exit the Rocky host shell to stop QEMU cleanly. This stops the VM without deleting its persistent overlay; make clean resets that host state. make demo-gate-9 uses the same operator workflow; make run-systemd remains as a compatibility alias, and make test-systemd-interactive is the automated regression.

The live test and interactive demonstration enable shared external networking. An upstream DNF update can take many minutes under QEMU TCG because every managed syscall is intercepted and audited. The offline systemd test uses only the prepared, digest-pinned cache.

Individual component and gate targets are documented in the Makefile and the corresponding files under docs/ and hdae/.

The primary adversary controls a process inside an instance. The host kernel, hardware, Ginux executable and approved configuration, boot chain, and operator are currently trusted. The balanced native backend still relies on the host for ELF loading, address spaces, page faults, signals, scheduling, and ptrace; those remain host-kernel attack surface.

Ginux is research software. It has not received independent security certification, does not provide complete Linux compatibility, and is not ready for production workloads. Unknown contract operations fail closed, but current coverage and guarantees are limited to the tested gates.

The precise supported claims, retained supervisor authority, trusted components, exclusions, compatibility gaps, performance limitation, and reproducible boundary tests are documented in Security boundary and limitations.

For agent containment, the protected object is the host and any authority not explicitly assigned to the instance. Ginux constrains the Linux processes in which an agent and its tools execute; it does not inspect model reasoning, secure an external model provider, or make untrusted code safe outside the enforced instance boundary.

The full intent, threat model, invariants, and gate plan live in:

Ginux is developed with Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE): human-owned product intent, architecture, constraints, and acceptance boundaries combined with agent-executed implementation, diagnosis, and test loops. Each approved gate records its scope, non-goals, acceptance criteria, verification, evidence, and stopping point in hdae/.

The independent bootable kernel remains available for research and historical reference:

It is no longer the active development line. The code remains available under the repository's existing terms for anyone who independently chooses to study or fork it.

The name remains a joke in the same family as Linux: Ginux combines Linux, GPT, and Greg. To keep the author's ego within its configured resource limit, the G officially stands for GPT.

Ginux is available under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE.

On x86-64 Linux, ginux launch <config> <root> [--result-file <fresh host path>] executes [instance].init with the configured arguments and environment inside the supplied host root directory. The bootstrap requires chroot and credential change privileges, and a kernel with close_range (Linux 5.9 or later). It drops to UID/GID 1000 before executing the workload. The configuration must select profile = "balanced" and backend = "ptrace-native"; storage and device assignments are not implemented by this command and are rejected.

[instance].workdir is optional and defaults to /work; / is also supported. The bootstrap creates the working directory if its parent exists, then enters it after dropping privileges. Init and working-directory paths are limited to 128 bytes and must be absolute without .. path components. Up to seven arguments of 128 bytes each and eight NAME=value environment entries of 256 bytes each are accepted. Invalid or oversized input fails before launch.

Workload stdout stays separate from supervisor diagnostics on stderr. Only stdin, stdout, and stderr are inherited by the workload. The launcher returns the workload exit code, or 128 + signal for signal termination. Startup failure returns 2; supervision or result-writing failure returns 1. Native fork, clone, and subsequent exec are unsupported; fork returns ENOSYS until child supervision is implemented. Non-x86-64 syscall ABIs and job-control group stops fail explicitly. Audit output is capped at 64 KiB plus a truncation notice. This path does not implement resource quotas from the instance metadata.

When requested, the result file is reserved exclusively before launch, with mode 0600 and a maximum path length of 512 bytes. Existing files are never overwritten. After completion, it contains one synced JSON object:

{"version":1,"outcome":"exited","code":0,"signal":null,"generation":null}

outcome is exited, signaled, or supervisor-error; only the relevant code or signal is populated. Storage generations are not implemented, so generation is null. A missing, empty, or malformed result is a protocol failure. A failure to write, sync, or close the result returns 1 even if the workload succeeded. Consumers should wait for launcher completion before reading it.

The focused Linux integration scenario consumes existing binaries:

make build make build-launch-fixture make build-gate1-fixture sudo make test-gate1-setup sudo make test-launch sudo make test-native-supervision

The separate process-native <config> <executable> command exercises native fork, clone, vfork, exec, threads, waits, termination signals, and pipes. It executes a trusted host fixture as the caller, without chroot; it does not require root on a host that permits tracing child processes. Configured launch remains a separate entry point and does not yet use this process loop.

Process creation returns virtual identities, including clone TID cells. Untraced, reparenting, namespace, and unsupported clone flags are denied. Thread slots are reclaimed on exit. CLONE_FILES shares one descriptor table; ordinary fork copies it, and exec unshares it before closing CLOEXEC entries. Worker-thread exec preserves the group's process identity. Inherited host files above stderr are closed before execution. PI futex operations and queries for another task's robust list are unsupported.

Build the fixtures explicitly, then run their independent scenarios:

make build build-process-fixtures make test-process-native make test-process-native SCENARIO=shared_pipe make test-process-native SCENARIO=thread_exec

The scenarios consume existing binaries under .artifacts/process, including checks for syscall ABI dispatch, clone restrictions, descriptor inheritance, thread reuse, successful and failed worker exec, signals, wait-status writes, nonblocking waits, and vfork. The existing native fork fixture also runs. These checks do not claim complete libc, job-control, or systemd compatibility.

entry.title: Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card
entry.content:
Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card On this page Summary

Iâve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, Iâve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards. Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I havenât specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG.

Hereâs how my âA100-80Gâ appears and functions.

NVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you more access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIAâs design allows one to relax restrictions by blowing more fuses!

In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. Iâve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here.

Acknowledgements

My work builds on prior research by Jon Pry and numerous others who have dedicated much of their time towards better understanding the GA100 die. I am disclosing my findings subsequent to another security researcher independently discovering the same vulnerability; I believe it to be in the best interest of the public to make this information publicly available. These findings were disclosed to NVIDIAâs product security team ahead of the publication of this article.

GA100 versions

The GA100 is an NVIDIA die that has been used to power almost 20 different SKUs - the A100 being the most well-known variant. I wonât delve into every SKU, but I will present the GA100 manifestations that matter to my work, covering the different versions of the CMP 170HX and the A100.

As fabbed, the GA100 die has 128 SMs, 12 FBPs, 5 NVDEC units, a PCIe Gen4 x16 controller, and depending on the framebuffer size, comes with 4-6 stacks of HBM co-packaged with the die. NVIDIA uses eFuses for yield-control and product segmentationâundifferentiated GA100s turn into more restrictive variants based on defect testing and manufacturer demand.

In one of the most extreme manifestations of product segmentation, the CMP 170HX, an Ethereum mining card with nominally 8 or 10 GB of application-exposed framebuffer capacity, actually comes with, respectively, ~80 and ~40 GB of HBM onboard! This work chiefly centers around how to fully unlock and use that capacity. Previous work has made great strides in unlocking the GA100 via software methods; VFI takes us across the last mile.

SKU Out-of-box Software (cmpunlocker) GA100VFI CMP 170HX 8GB Framebuffer 8 GB 64 GB 64-80 GB1 CMP 170HX 10GB Framebuffer 10 GB 40 GB2 40-48 GB Both CMPs SMs 70 70 120-128 PCIe generation 1 2 4 NVLink No No Yes3 ECC No No Yes4 Multi-Instance GPUs No No Yes4 NVDEC 0 0 54
Hardware restrictions

So, how does NVIDIA utilize fuses to produce both a datacenter A100 and a mining CMP card from one die? To understand this, we need to take a closer look at the fuse controller located on the GA100.

The fuse controller is a block that contains 16,384 eFuses (512 rows of 32) and a bunch of logic surrounding that raw fuse macro. Its job is to perform fuse readout and programming, protect the underlying fuses, and provide usable âoption wordsâ to the rest of the die. These option words subsequently decide how the die functions and what features are enabled.

Each eFuse can be in one of two states (blown=1, unblown=0), and the 512 rows are divided into 4 regions:

Regular fuses (rows 0-221). These are straightforward; often single (pairs of) fuses will map to an option word, such as OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM (an option word that determines whether further fuse programming is allowed or not). Regular fuses have built-in redundancy: for example, OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM consists of a PRI and RED (primary and redundant) fuse, in this case the primary instance is fuse 0 of row 0, and the redundant is fuse 0 of row 1. Some option words are scalars, such as OPT_X_COORDINATE, which is 9 bits wide and ostensibly holds the x-coordinate of the die on the fabbed wafer. Importantly, if a regular fuse is blown, there is basically no remedy to persistently unblow it (save for RIR later). Fuseless fuses (rows 222-487). This is a weird one. Apparently NVIDIA got frustrated with accidentally blowing regular fuses and ruining their engineering samples, and came up with a system to encode effective option words in a JTAG chain-like format (see this patent). Think about FF as essentially a script that describes what option words should have what values. FF fuses (excuse the RAS syndrome) concern most of the functionality we can unlock using VFI. This is because FF option words can be trivially cleared by simply writing new FF rows! Weâll about this more in depth, later. For now, you should know that NVIDIA also knows this, because under normal conditions, you are strictly prevented from performing any FF fuse blows. IFF fuses (rows 487-512). These contain instructions in a different format than the FF one. Theyâre out of scope for this post, and theyâre mainly useful for on-the-fly reprogramming of fuse controller option words. They are usually not accessible in a production card. RIR fuses (8 rows of 32 fuses, which are technically not part of the 512 rows). These are provided by the designer of the fuse macro (TSMC datasheet here) and are essentially the first party designerâs intended âfuse repairâ mechanism. The RIR section on a GA100 has space for 16 repair instructions, each overriding the value of an identified single fuse in the main 512 rows. Unfortunately for us, specifically in the 8 GB 170HX SKU, 15 of the 16 RIR words are all ones, and the 16th word encodes a useless repair instruction that can only be rarely leveraged for any interesting unlock. The story is different for the 10 GB SKU, but thatâs a matter for another dayâ¦

There are two really interesting groups of fuses for the VFI-based unlock:

âControl fusesâ. The term comes from NVIDIAâs Tegra hardware headers, they use it to refer specifically to rows 0 and 1, which specify the values of highly security-sensitive option words. Fuseless fuses, which encode all of the interesting option words that decide whether a GA100 is born to be a measly mining card or an AI datacenter workhorse.

Before we name some of the FF-encoded option words, weâll have to first understand the FF record format in a bit more detail, then talk about the die blocks that govern the features we are interested in.

Fuseless fuses

Each FF row is a 32-bit record. Bits 0â4 select a chain, bit 5 distinguishes FF from IFF (0 for FF), bits 6â15 select a 16-bit block, and bits 16â31 supply that blockâs new value. The JTAG-chain picture from the patent is quite literal here: the controller builds the option data by replaying these records into chains. Fixed locations in each chain correspond to individual option words.

If two records address the same chain and block, the later record wins. For example, 0x0fe805c1 means chain 1, block 23, data 0x0fe8. Appending that record can clear an effective bit set by an earlier FF record. No physical fuse is unblown; a new row replaces the old 16-bit block. This works for FF-backed options, not the regular control fuses in rows 0 and 1.

Now that we know how FF words are encoded, hereâs a list of the interesting words and their locations. These were discovered by a particularly helpful researcher who cross-compared FF values and effective option words from different GA100 SKUs in order to differentially understand the FF chain/block to option word mappings, as there is no known official mapping.

Named option Inferred FF location Use NV_FUSE_OPT_FBIO_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 83â106; blocks 5â6 Memory I/O floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_FBPA_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 107â130; blocks 6â8 Memory subpartition floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_GPC_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 131â138; block 8 GPC floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC0_DISABLE through NV_FUSE_OPT_TPC_GPC7_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 187+8i through 194+8i for GPC i; blocks 11â15 Eight TPC masks NV_FUSE_OPT_PES_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 251â274; blocks 15â17 PES floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_FBP_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 307â318; block 19 Framebuffer partition floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_ROP_L2_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 319â342; blocks 19â21 ROP/L2 floorsweep NV_FUSE_OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE Chain 1 bits 368â370; block 23 NVLink disable mask NV_FUSE_OPT_DISABLE_GEN3_SPEED Chain 2 block 39; which of bits 1 and 9 is unresolved PCIe Gen3 speed restriction NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_MAGIC_BITS_D[25] Chain 2 block 47 bit 3 Gen4 speed-disable flag NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN23_DISABLE Chain 2 block 49 bit 6 PCIe boot policy NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_BOOT_GEN3_DISABLE Chain 2 block 49 bit 7 PCIe boot policy NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_DEVIDA Chain 2, bits 593â608; blocks 37â38 Device identity NV_FUSE_OPT_PCIE_DEVIDB Chain 2, bits 609â624; blocks 38â39 Device identity NV_FUSE_OPT_SYS_PIPE_DISABLE Chain 1, bits 372â379; block 23 Multi-instance GPU enabled pipes

The acronyms FBIO/FBPA/FBP/TPC/GPC/PES/ROP all refer to microarchitectural elements, please see this diagram from the GA100 whitepaper to further understand how these are related to each other:

FBP is the internal NVIDIA term for a âframebuffer partitionâ, with 2 FBPs to one HBM stack. FBPAs are subpartitions, 2 FBPAs to one FBP. PES/ROP are blocks (seemingly graphics-related) that are required for an SM to function.

With this knowledge in hand, what if we could write new FF rows that set the _DISABLE words to be all zeroes, or at least, as permissive as possible given die defects? If we look at how the _DISABLE options are used in conjunction with other elements, weâll quickly see that these _DISABLE words are the primary lever we have in preventing parts of the die from being âfloorsweptâ. After illuminating the âwhat-ifâ, Iâll talk about the âhowâ: the exact application of voltage fault injection and the fuse controller safeguards we can defeat with VFI.

Floorsweeping

NVIDIA puts these options in charge of setting floorsweep signals, which will render a die element unreachable (and likely powered down). From experiments, I believe the floorsweep lines are specified in RTL, emanating from the fuse controller and terminating in individual functional blocks and controlling some master power/clock domain switch within the block. I have observed the floorsweeping behavior to correspond with very little latency with the value of the fuse controllerâs effective status words for each functional block.

Letâs take FBP floorsweeping, for example. On one of my 8 GB cards, OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852: FBPs 1, 4, 6, and 11 were masked. The separate OPT_FBP_DEFECTIVE mask was 0x840, covering 6 and 11. After I reduced the FF-backed disable mask to 0x840 with a replacement FF row, the extra masks on 1 and 4 were gone, but the defective 6 and 11 stayed disabled. That leaves 10 of the dieâs 12 FBPs in the effective mask. Functionally, FBPs 1 and 4, which refused register reads and writes when OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852, became responsive after this fuse write.

Although the functional blocks can be âunfloorsweptâ with FF writes, this does not fully suffice to render the block fully available to an end application - the default framebuffer geometry configuration uses only a portion of each available HBM stack, for example.

To bypass that, we can utilize what is essentially a small modification to cmpunlockerâs method. The usual driver patch for the 8 -> 64 GB unlocks writes to a particular set of feature configuration words (FBPA_CFG, SM_SPEED_SELECT, etc.). The default values are chosen to succeed for the commonly found variant of the 170HX, which has the _DISABLE FF-derived option words preventing certain functional blocks from being used (any attempt to use them will return floorswept errors). With the unlocking FF burns in place, we can write even more permissive words into the configuration registers, resulting in what is functionally an A100-80G.

Achieving the FF burn

With the information we have, it seems straightforward that if one could blow arbitrary FF fuses, any GA100 could be fully unlocked to its maximum capability, as determined by die yield and the populated memory stacks. But how do we blow FF fuses? Letâs take a look at the fuse programming functionality of the fuse controller to understand more.

To request a fuse blow, one must write to the FUSEADDR, FUSEWDATA, and FUSECTRL registers belonging to the fuse controller. Although not nominally accessible to the host or to unprivileged requesters, with the Canary in the Crypto Mine ROP, opening up the responsible privilege level masks is trivial. And so, many researchers have attempted to coerce the fuse controller to blow fuses in the FF region. Some of our shared observations follow:

The fuse controller has an internal FSM, and it indicates its current state via the FUSECTRL_STATE bits. The fuse controller enters a WRITE_PROGRAM state per each âhotâ bit in the requested FUSEWDATA value. This tracks with the expected fuse programming behavior. However, unless a specific option word is cleared, writes to fuse addresses outside of the FPF range (rows 96-221) do not actually take place. Fuses in this region (believed to be âfield programmable fusesâ indicating a watermark of which ucode versions have run, alongside other field-relevant information) do take effect, and the fuse controller state machine behaves identically between FPF and non-FPF regions.

The specific option word I am referring to is OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE (âSBFEâ), and it is set to be 1 in all production cards. When this option word is clear, fuse programming is allowed in any address. When it is set, only FPF fuses may be blown. To date, no one has found any way to burn FF fuses with SBFE=1, even when operating the fuse controller from HS contexts. It is not clear what âsecured burnâ truly means, I speculate that there must be a software-only way to perform non-FPF burns even with SBFE=1, and we just donât know what the âsecuredâ adjective really means here.

Note PLM, HS, ucode, â¦; I am delving into using a bunch of NVIDIA-specific terminology in this section as the explanation gets deeper. For a really in-depth explanation of what these mean, I refer you to other sources such as Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon.

Importantly, as people have figured out on more permissive cards, it is possible to perform FF burns with SBFE=0! And as it turns out, achieving this state is how we achieve the GA100 unlock. After much trial-and-error, I have resorted to inducing this state via voltage fault injection, and I was able to achieve it. Letâs talk some more about voltage glitching.

Voltage fault injection

Much has been said about VFI, and Iâll leave the in-depth explanation to other sources. In short, applying brief pulses of low supply voltage will often cause unexpected behavior in integrated circuits. I asked GPT-6 Astra to design an STM32G4 based board that taps into the PWMVID signal on the CMP PCB. PWMVID is an NVIDIA standard for voltage regulators, and my glitcher intercepts the PWM signal emitted by the GA100 die, and replaces it with its own waveform fed into the MP2888B VRM driver IC. With my setup, I can induce the cardâs own VRM to produce timed glitches for me, which is simpler than MOSFET-based setups and enables faster glitching than attempting to directly drive the PMBus.

The glitcher requires two connections to the PCB, ideally done with magnet/enameled wire. One wire taps NVVDD for voltage sensing, and another wire taps the PWMVID signal. The only other required step for the glitcher to function is the removal of a 0402 0ohm resistor, which will break the connection between the GA100 output PWM pin and the VRM IC. Finding where to place the taps is trivial by tracing the pinout of the MP2888B, specifically its PWMVID and VOSEN pins (the MP2888B shares a footprint with its sibling public chip MP2888A). Test points directly adjacent to the MP2888B enable relatively easy installation of the PWMVID tap.

With this tap in place, a single glitch attempt involves this sequence:

Remove card power Apply card power Start a timer (âglitch timerâ) as soon as NVVDD crosses a threshold Execute a proposed voltage waveform by issuing a PWMVID signal, aligned to the glitch timer Observe card behavior, repeat from step 1 as needed

My setup achieves steps 1/2 with a simple ACPI S0 -> S3 -> S0 transition, which can be done in a few seconds on a modern desktop platform. More intrusive modifications or expensive rigs can probably achieve a better experiment rate, but in my experience this setup suffices to unlock cards in somewhere between 1 hour and 48 hours of glitching time using the approach described later.

For the NVVDD threshold, the Astra-authored firmware uses an STM32 comparator to detect when NVVDD crosses 225mV, after which a tight DMA loop drives the desired duties on the PWMVID pin. After S0, the host inspects the card state and decides what to do next; if it involves another glitch, the glitcher board will be commanded over USB with a glitch pattern. Then the host induces S3 with an RTC timer to wake back up in ~3s (empirically derived period for decent stability).

Sometimes the host will fail to return to S0, Iâve remedied this with relegating bookkeeping and glitch campaign preparation to an SBC (Radxa Cubie A5E) which also can drive the motherboard power/reset button pins via GPIO if the glitch target host is unresponsive.

More specifics are shared in the GA100VFI repository if youâre interested. For now, letâs take a look at the different interesting states we can trigger via VFI, as well as the specific glitch state that we need to burn FF rows. To help illuminate the differences between each glitch state, I have built an empirical model of how the fuse controller starts up when voltage is applied. Note that without the RTL that implements the fuse controller, all we have are guesses. Here are the hypothesized boot stages:

Sense RIR, as required by the fuse macro Sense (from fuse macro into readout register) control rows Latch control rows into control row-derived option words Sense remaining rows Latch regular fuse values into their option words Parse FF chain Latch FF chain values into their option words

These hypothetical stages are based on what I can actually read from the die: controller states, raw rows when CMD_READ works, the published option words, and whether the PRI ring can still reach the rest of the GPU. By looking at a few key values, we can tell glitch outcomes apart. Importantly, glitch patterns and outcomes are very much die-specific, so consider these example waveforms and responses to be just that, examples. Letâs take a look at 3 interesting glitch states.

1. All fuses sensed as zero

Some glitches make almost every published option word read as zero. In one captured state, 669 of 672 named option reads were zero; the other three were error responses. The controllerâs CRC status was 0x00 (not parsed yet), the PCIe ID read as 2080 (the base GA100 PCIe product ID, does not correspond to a real retail product), and the GPUâs PRI ring was held in reset.

This state is consistent with a catastrophic failure on behalf of the fuse controller. The card comes up basically unusable, because almost all boot functions are disrupted by the all-zero state. However, interesting enough, the card trains at PCIe Gen4 natively! Some slightly altered variants may showcase sections of fuses being successfully latched, or containing garbled values instead of all-zeroes. I was not able to push any of these states towards an FF burn; in almost all of them the fuse controller is unreachable or dysfunctional.

2. RIR read disrupted

Reading the RIR data on the CMP 170HX 8GB reveals its exact effect: 15 noop repair instructions, and one write that changes the value of a fuse in row 18, whose option word we can monitor. Further, because the RIR sense is consumed internally by the fuse macro instead of directly by the fuse controller, we can observe a disrupted RIR latch by attempting to read the raw row - the observed bitflip remains consistent across the flipped option word as well as the raw fuse row. This sets an interesting chronological checkpoint in investigating die boot (RIR sense must happen prior to other fuse sensing), but is not a useful glitch in itself.

3. Goldilockâs glitch

The successful three-pulse state on my first card seemed to disrupt precisely the row0/1 based option words, while leaving other fuses and option words intact. In this state, all of the row0/1 derived option words are zero. The initial readbacks look like this:

Signal Initial readback PCI ID and access 20c2; BAR0 and the PRI ring respond FUSECTRL 0xe0040000 (IDLE) CRC_STATUS 0x55 (both halves parsed without errors) DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE 0 OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE 0 ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM 0 FUSECTRL/FUSEOPT privilege masks 0xffffffff for both Raw rows 0 and 1 Both still 0x53557c3d, unchanged from before the glitch

At this stage, we are still not yet capable of issuing FF writes, because ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0. I am honestly not sure why ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM would ever be zero, given itâs 1 in retail boards, so this almost reads to me like a way to implement a glitch-detection canary (or at least it would be elegant to do so).

Fuse sensing happens one row at a time, with all 32 fuses powered for sensing with one line, meaning it is much more challenging for an attacker to make a single fuse appear as cleared or set. It would make sense, then, to include a âcanaryâ fuse that disables security-critical features (like fuse burning) when it is cleared, because usually the attacker can only manipulate fuse sensing at the row granularity at most. So, when the row0/1 option words come up as all cleared, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0 stops us from burning any fuses.

However, take a look at what we have in this state: DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE=0. This word is normally 1, and it stops us from setting the EN_SW_OVERRIDE register to 1, which then lets us âshadowâ most of the option words exposed by the fuse controller. Doing so involves writing to a register CTRL_OPT_*, corresponding to option word OPT_*, which then determines the effective value STATUS_OPT_*. This is what lets us shadow SBFE to be 0. But, even though we have DSOV=0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM turns out to be one of the option words that are impossible to shadow, even with DSOV=0. So it seems weâre stuck.

At least thatâs what I thought, and I banged my head against the wall in this state for a while. Then I noticed that there is one fuse controller command I havenât tried issuing yet: SENSE_CTRL. I had refrained from issuing this, because on the face of it it seems like all of the row0/1 (control fuse) derived option words would match their fused values, which would reset SBFE, turn off software option word shadowing, and leave us unable to fuse. To my surprise, when I issued this command, all of the control-fuse-derived options went to their fused value, except DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE, which remained 0!

With DSOV=0, we can trivially set SBFE to 0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM is 1 because it matches its fused value, and we are off to the races! One wrinkle remains in that FUSEWDATA may have a locked down PLM, but with DSOV=0, we can just write 0 to OPT_SECURE_FUSE_WDATA_WR_SECURE to set the PLM to be all-ones, opening host access for fusing.

At this point, all thatâs left to do is to calculate _DISABLE words that match the _DEFECTIVE values for the features we are interested in, and issue FF burns. Note that the occupied FF space and defective bits differ per die, so each burn must be die-tailored.

End results Framebuffer unlock

On 8 GB cards with 80 GB intact (seems to be around ~90% of 8 GB cards from my limited sample size), the unlock yields the full 80 GB as a usable framebuffer. Multiple synthetic tests (writing pseudorandom words throughout the full framebuffer and reading them back after L2 invalidation) as well as real workloads (such as vLLM and SGLand) are fully functional. As mentioned, one of my cards has only 64 GB intact. In this case, the hardware unlock yields no framebuffer advantage.

Compute unlock

The 170HX is limited to 70 SMs out of the box. In practice, there are almost always >120 SMs non-defective on the die, and the unlock allows using them all. This results in a significant performance uplift, ~1.7x compared to the software-only 170HX unlock, and even an impressive ~1.2x over a retail A100!

PCIe generation

The only thing that stops cmpunlocker from advancing beyond PCIe Gen2 are the FF option words. With relevant bits cleared, Gen3/4 train and are confirmed to be fully functional. When combined with the PCIe decoupling capacitor mod, up to PCIe Gen4 x16 is attainable, matching a retail A100 PCIe variant.

NVLink

Zeroing out the OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE word is only one of the required mods for NVLink to actually work. Because the CMP 170HX PCB is missing the U11 IC (which connects PCIe 3.3v to an NVLink bridge pin), a stock board fails to bring up the reference clock generator on attached NVLink bridges. Simply bridging two of the pins on the footprint of U11 resolves this issue, although it removes whatever regulation or protection was provided by U11. Be careful if youâre bridging GPUs powered by different power supplies, as this will connect the +3.3V rails together unless you leave U11 unpopulated on some of your GPUs! The NVLink bridge works fine if you just patch U11 on one of the boards in the pair.

On the firmware side of NVLink enablement, there is a ROM check that needs to be bypassed with additional host-side commands. Iâm sure your clanker can figure it out ;)

While investigating the NVLink unlock, I also found a few interesting quirks with NVIDIAâs NVLink implementation on the GA100. I will be posting a further blog post on this, so stay tuned!

Future directions

With arbitrary fuse burning, we mostly gain feature unlocks. Some security-sensitive options are shipped unblown by default, and burning them may lead to interesting footholds. But whatâs more interesting to me are the deeper glitch states where many default-blown security-sensitive fuses sense unblown, enabling routes like debug HS execution, which grant unprecedented access to die internals.

References Jon Pry, A Canary in the Crypto Mine: Defeating Stack Protection in a GPU Secure Coprocessor (2026). Amogh Munikote, cmpunlocker (2026). Otto Bittner et al., The Forgotten Threat of Voltage Glitching: A Case Study on Nvidia Tegra X2 SoCs (2021). NVIDIA, US9230678B2: Integrated circuit having an enhanced fuseless fuse structure (2016). TSMC, TEF07F32X32HD18_PHRM_C180518 electrical fuse datasheet, rev. 120A (2018). hexkyz and SciresM, Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon (2021). TechPowerUp, NVIDIA GA100 GPU specifications. GA100VFI source repository. Footnotes

Anecdotally, out of the 10 specimens of CMP 170HX 8 GB I have examined, only one has shipped with only 64 GB usable, the rest all have a functional framebuffer size of 80 GB. â©

Although the Canary in the Crypto Mine paper claims a stable 80 GB on the 10 GB SKU, very few, if any, cards in the wild have been able to achieve this, and solid evidence is scarce. It remains plausible that some number of 10 GB SKUs really do come shipped with 80 GB on-board, however the percentage seems very low according to the community. Most âunstableâ 80 GB unlocks are explained with a combination of L2 caching and memory aliasing over a true 40 GB framebuffer. â©

Enabling NVLink further requires a very small hardware mod due to a missing component on the 170HX PCB, Iâll talk more about this later. â©

Untested. â© â©2 â©3

entry.title: Physically Controllable Relighting of Photographs
entry.content:
Physically Controllable Relighting of Photographs

Patent pending

Abstract

We present a self-supervised approach to in-the-wild image relighting that enables fully controllable, physically based illumination editing. We achieve this by combining the physical accuracy of traditional rendering with the photorealistic appearance made possible by neural rendering. Our pipeline works by inferring a colored mesh representation of a given scene using monocular estimates of geometry and intrinsic components. This representation allows users to define their desired illumination configuration in 3D. The scene under the new lighting can then be rendered using a path-tracing engine. We send this approximate rendering of the scene through a feed-forward neural renderer to predict the final photorealistic relighting result. We develop a differentiable rendering process to reconstruct in-the-wild scene illumination, enabling self-supervised training of our neural renderer on raw image collections. Our method represents a significant step in bringing the explicit physical control over lights available in typical 3D computer graphics tools, such as Blender, to in-the-wild relighting.

ACM Transactions on Graphics (Proc. SIGGRAPH Asia), 2024 Best Paper Award Honorable Mention

Intrinsic image decomposition aims to separate the surface reflectance and the effects from the illumination given a single photograph. Due to the complexity of the problem, most prior works assume a single-color illumination and a Lambertian world, which limits their use in illumination-aware image editing applications. In this work, we separate an input image into its diffuse albedo, colorful diffuse shading, and specular residual components. We arrive at our result by gradually removing first the single-color illumination and then the Lambertian-world assumptions. We show that by dividing the problem into easier sub-problems, in-the-wild colorful diffuse shading estimation can be achieved despite the limited ground-truth datasets. Our extended intrinsic model enables illumination-aware analysis of photographs and can be used for image editing applications such as specularity removal and per-pixel white balancing.

ACM Transactions on Graphics, 2023

Intrinsic decomposition is a fundamental mid-level vision problem that plays a crucial role in various inverse rendering and computational photography pipelines. Generating highly accurate intrinsic decompositions is an inherently under-constrained task that requires precisely estimating continuous-valued shading and albedo. In this work, we achieve high-resolution intrinsic decomposition by breaking the problem into two parts. First, we present a dense ordinal shading formulation using a shift- and scale-invariant loss in order to estimate ordinal shading cues without restricting the predictions to obey the intrinsic model. We then combine low- and high-resolution ordinal estimations using a second network to generate a shading estimate with both global coherency and local details. We encourage the model to learn an accurate decomposition by computing losses on the estimated shading as well as the albedo implied by the intrinsic model. We develop a straightforward method for generating dense pseudo ground truth using our models predictions and multi-illumination data, enabling generalization to in-the-wild imagery. We present exhaustive qualitative and quantitative analysis of our predicted intrinsic components against state-of-the-art methods. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world applicability of our estimations by performing otherwise difficult editing tasks such as recoloring and relighting.

Despite significant advancements in network-based image harmonization techniques, there still exists a domain disparity between typical training pairs and real-world composites encountered during inference. Most existing methods are trained to reverse global edits made on segmented image regions, which fail to accurately capture the lighting inconsistencies between the foreground and background found in composited images. In this work, we introduce a self-supervised illumination harmonization approach formulated in the intrinsic image domain. First, we estimate a simple global lighting model from mid-level vision representations to generate a rough shading for the foreground region. A network then refines this inferred shading to generate a harmonious re-shading that aligns with the background scene. In order to match the color appearance of the foreground and background, we utilize ideas from prior harmonization approaches to perform parameterized image edits in the albedo domain. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we present results from challenging real-world composites and conduct a user study to objectively measure the enhanced realism achieved compared to state-of-the-art harmonization methods.
